strings.quiz.answer.label: Answer:
strings.quiz.q1.question: One chatbot question uses about as much electricity as a microwave running for…
strings.quiz.q1.explanation: Google measured 0.24 Wh for a typical Gemini text prompt. A microwave uses that in under a second. Chatting is cheap.
strings.quiz.q2.question: One heavy coding-agent prompt uses as much energy as how many chatbot questions?
strings.quiz.q2.explanation: Coding agents re-read their whole context thousands of times. One researcher's Claude Code logs came to ~150 Wh per prompt. That's about 9 minutes of microwave.
strings.quiz.q3.question: How much did RAM contract prices go up in the first 3 months of 2026?
strings.quiz.q3.explanation: AI data centers need huge amounts of memory, so chipmakers moved production to AI chips. Everyone else pays more. Another +58–63% was expected the next quarter.
strings.quiz.q4.question: How much water does one chatbot question use?
strings.quiz.q4.explanation: Google says ~5 drops (0.26 mL), counting only cooling inside the data center. Researchers who also count the water used by power plants get much bigger numbers. Both measure something real.
strings.quiz.q5.question: What share of US electricity will data centers use by 2030?
strings.quiz.q5.explanation: Data centers used 4.4% in 2023. Berkeley Lab now projects about 12% by 2030 (range 9.5–15%).
strings.method.meta.title: Show your work · Token Damage
strings.method.meta.description: Where every number on a Token Damage receipt comes from: prices, the electricity method, and the satire formulas.
strings.method.title: Show your work
strings.method.intro: Every number on a receipt carries one of four labels. This page shows where each one comes from. It is meant to be boring.
strings.method.tiers.heading: The four labels
strings.method.tier.measured: No mark: measured. Read from your logs. Exact counts.
strings.method.tier.priced: ≡ Priced: public API list price × measured tokens. What the same usage would cost at list price, not what you paid.
strings.method.tier.estimated: ≈ Estimated: always a range, at most two significant figures, with the method below.
strings.method.tier.satire: ✶ Satire: made up on purpose. Always red, always labeled as made up.
strings.method.stamp: Every receipt is stamped with the method version and the date of its prices.
strings.method.prices.heading: Prices
strings.method.prices.intro: List prices in USD per million tokens, as of {date}. They are checked against the providers' price pages before every release.
strings.method.prices.fallback: A model missing from the table is priced as the closest listed one and marked *. A model with no listed family says "not priced", never $0.
strings.method.energy.heading: Electricity (method v1)
strings.method.energy.body: Providers publish no per-token energy figures for these models. We use per-token coefficients by token type, calibrated so that one published Claude Code log (3.2 billion tokens, 96% cache reads) reproduces its author's central estimate of 170 kWh. The low and high ends follow the author's 70–330 kWh range.
strings.method.energy.readNote: Cache reads are the largest uncertainty: bounds of 1% to 25% of a fresh token.
strings.method.energy.anchors: Sanity checks: about 50 kWh per billion agent tokens (20–100), and about 41 Wh for a median Claude Code session. A result far outside these means the parser is wrong, not the world.
strings.method.detail.heading: Water and CO₂
strings.method.detail.body: Shown in the detail view only, never on the share card. Water for on-site cooling: kWh × 0.2–2 L/kWh. Off-site water is larger and disputed; it is shown as a separate note and never added in. CO₂e: kWh × 0.34–0.42 kg/kWh (US, location-based); market-based figures run lower.
strings.method.satire.heading: Satire formulas
strings.method.satire.body: RAM-X, your share of the shortage: tokens ÷ 60 trillion × 0.95 × 0.42 dollars per stick. 60 trillion is Meta's reported 30-day token usage, 0.95 the Q1 2026 rise in DRAM contract prices, and 0.42 the Coefficient of Vibes. The formula is absurd on purpose. The price rise is real. That you caused it is not.
strings.method.sources.heading: Sources
strings.method.sources.intro: Citations stay in their original language.
strings.privacy.meta.title: Privacy · Token Damage
strings.privacy.meta.description: What Token Damage reads, what it never reads, and what leaves your computer: only what you choose to share.
strings.privacy.title: Privacy
strings.privacy.intro: Short version: it runs on your computer, and nothing leaves it unless you share it.
strings.privacy.reads.heading: What it reads
strings.privacy.reads.body: The usage records your AI coding agents already keep on your computer: Claude Code in ~/.claude, Codex in ~/.codex, Gemini CLI in ~/.gemini/tmp, OpenCode in ~/.local/share/opencode. From them it counts tokens, model calls, times and the number of words you typed, then prints a receipt.
strings.privacy.never.heading: What it never reads or keeps
strings.privacy.never.body: It never reads your code. It never keeps your prompts: words are counted in memory and the text is discarded. It never stores project names, folder paths, branch names or file names. It makes no network requests. There is no account and no telemetry.
strings.privacy.stored.heading: What it stores on your computer
strings.privacy.stored.body: One file, ~/.token-damage/state.json: a run counter and which adjuster's notes it used recently, so the next receipt doesn't repeat them. Numbers only, never text. Delete it any time.
strings.privacy.leaves.heading: What leaves your computer
strings.privacy.leaves.body: Only a receipt you choose to share: an image, or a link whose numbers live in the link itself, after the #. Browsers never send that part to any server, so this site never sees your numbers.
strings.privacy.site.heading: This website
strings.privacy.site.body: No cookies, no analytics, no accounts. Fonts are served from this site.
strings.privacy.affiliation: Token Damage is not affiliated with Anthropic, OpenAI, Google or the makers of OpenCode. Product names are used to describe compatibility.
strings.privacy.source: The code is open source, so you can check all of this yourself.
